column2: Sitting on the dock deep in conversation, they see everyone run at the sound of the bell (“Pavlov's dogs,” says Elaine). Arriving twenty minutes later: all the food has disappeared. Never late again afterward. 20 minutes late; not a crumb of food left Consequences: They become sprinters at every bell

They meet up with the Grippes, Cage, and Cunningham. Merce announces a two-hour dance class six mornings a week; Elaine signs up on the spot. Albers confides that there are too many invited speakers: Fuller and Lippold had declined and been replaced by Charles Burchard and Peter Grippe, then they announced they were coming after all. Some teachers are absent from the get-acquainted party at the Alberses'. Albers foresees “complications”; Elaine easily remembers the students' first names but forgets those of the faculty, referring to them by trade and figure Consequences: The first signs of the summer's quarrels

Bill's class: about ten students. Albers's course on color theory and Cunningham's course: about thirty each. Dressed-up evening lectures: Winslow Ames (printmaking), Beaumont Newhall (photography), Isaac Rosenfeld (Tolstoy), Erwin Bodky (Beethoven), Edgar Kaufmann Jr. (industrial design).

Fuller, short, stocky, dapper, improvises moving geometric constructions with bobby pins, clothespins, and five-and-dime objects, folds an icosahedron into a tetrahedron, declares the square, the cube, and the numbers two and ten obsolete (with a history of ciphering punished by death in the Middle Ages), extols nine and three, the circle, the triangle, the tetrahedron, the sphere, theories of ecology and engineering. At the blackboard: “here's our old friend, the hypotenuse” — Elaine decides at once to take his classes Consequences: Elaine enrolls in Fuller's classes

Fuller shows two irregular pieces of metal that form a perfect cube if fitted together correctly. The students pass them around for an hour and a half without success. Bill comes in, weighs them in his hand, and fits them together on the first try. Bill later explains: since the engineers had tried every logical way, he looked for “the least logical way” Consequences: Fuller, a believer in artists' intuition, approves without surprise

Albers, passing by, hears Fuller using the specialized vocabulary of the automobile engine and tells him they do not understand what he is saying. General laughter; Albers recovers by specifying that he meant Elaine.

After breakfast, Bill joins his students; Elaine takes Cunningham's dance class from 8 to 10 a.m.; some mornings from 10 to noon she attends Albers's color course; in the evening, she imitates “Juppy” for Bill. dance class 8:00-10:00; color 10:00-12:00; the nickname Juppy given by Anni Albers

At first at a loss in the emptiness of the cottage, Bill fills the walls with pastels for two weeks, then tapes a 25 x 32-inch sheet onto a board on the easel and paints in oil, scraping off the excess pigment every evening to keep the surface fresh. Blazing pinks, oranges, and yellows sweep across the sheet and crystallize into an image — which he invariably destroys. a 25 x 32 in. sheet; daily scraping; images Elaine loved “blasted away” Consequences: This is the process that produced the canvases of his first exhibition in the spring of 1948; it culminates in “Asheville”

More parties in two months than in the five preceding years: small cocktail parties in the student studios, big evenings in the faculty cottages, a grand final ball at which Elaine waltzes with Bucky. One night, Bill flees a noisy party to walk: ten minutes on, no more lights or sounds, a velvety black sky and stars; Bill wants to go back: “The universe gives me the creeps.” Bucky's compliment while waltzing: “You're a terrific performance per ounce!”

A rainy day; the whole campus outside the project watches; the students bolt the slats together; Fuller confides to Elaine that it will not work; a countdown; the dome rises a few feet and collapses; the Bauhaus people laugh Words: Fuller: it won't work, but let's try anyway; Elaine: she knew that Bucky was right and that they were all wrong Atmosphere: Rain, collective suspense, mocking laughter, Elaine's faith Stakes: Public failure as teaching; Black Mountain's spirit of salvage against Bauhaus aestheticism

Bill fills the emptiness of the cottage with pastels for weeks, then paints in oil on 25x32-inch paper, scraping off the pigment every evening; the blazing pinks and oranges finally crystallize into an image — and he blasts it away, again and again. Atmosphere: frenzy, Elaine's familiar pain Stakes: Creative dissatisfaction as method

Fuller has students unload his aluminum trailer: origami-space models of tetrahedrons, icosahedrons, domes, pyramids; despite the exhausting drive from New York, he gives a three-hour lecture on the end of the era of the square Words: Lippold: like meeting Zoroaster speaking Islamic; Cunningham: immediate and absolute adoration and love Atmosphere: Mixed fascination: traveling salesman, prophet, eccentric futurist, possible charlatan Stakes: Fuller's charisma takes hold of the college

Before a Satie recital, Cage gives a short speech denouncing the centrality of Beethoven and the German harmonic tradition before an audience of former Bauhaus members who hold them in high esteem, and praises duration in Satie Atmosphere: Fury in the hall Stakes: The war of musical lineages, German against French

De Kooning, in the emptiness of the cottage, feverishly turns out pastels for a few weeks until the walls are covered; then he fixes a large sheet on an easel and moves on to oil. Words: Elaine: “He was in a vacuum that he began to fill with pastels”. Atmosphere: a fever of work in a bare room Stakes: The birth of Asheville

On learning of Gorky's death (July 21), de Kooning shuts himself away for days; he tells his student Pat Passlof that now he has a chance. Words: “Now I have a chance”. Atmosphere: grief and release mingled Stakes: The dead mentor's legacy hovers over Asheville.

The car empties as the journey goes on; Ray gets up and joins the two men at the back; introductions; Cage announces that Tobey is ill and has been replaced by de Kooning. Words: Cage: Tobey is ill, another artist is replacing him. — Who? — De Kooning. Atmosphere: A luminous chance, a beautiful train ride, summery Stakes: The improvisation of BMC's hiring, so typical of its policy

During the summer's rural stay, Elaine reads passages of Kierkegaard to Bill; Patricia Passlof, who was there, remembers it decades later. The idyll ends with the arrival of the news of Gorky's suicide. Words: Of Gorky, de Kooning will later say: he was a peasant, very strong; when his body betrayed him, he got rid of it. Atmosphere: Rural intimacy, readings aloud, then grief falling on the summer. Stakes: The shift from a summer of creative utopia to the grief and existential despair that will feed “A Desperate View”.

Two irregular pieces of metal pass from hand to hand for an hour and a half; Bill comes in; Fuller asks him, as someone from another discipline, to try; Bill weighs, observes, fits them together — a perfect cube on the first try; Bucky nods without surprise; Elaine amazed Words: Bucky: let's see what an artist can do. Bill later: he looked for the least logical way Atmosphere: amused astonishment Stakes: intuition against logic
Four months after the Egan exhibition closes, the Museum of Modern Art buys Painting for $750. $750 Consequences: The first financial relief after a failure to sell

Cage stages Satie's play: Elaine plays Frisette, daughter of Baron Méduse; Fuller plays the baron; Schrager, Frisette's suitor; Cunningham a mechanical monkey; Arthur Penn directs. Performance on August 14 in the dining hall (there is no theater at the college), the high point of the summer session. Cage plays on an out-of-tune piano. the monkey's sixty-second dances; an out-of-tune piano; the performance on August 14 Consequences: There is talk of taking the production to New York, but no one knows any influential sponsors; the sets and costumes go to Manhattan.

Fuller fears making a fool of himself as a puffed-up baron in tails; Penn uses deliberately silly exercises — hopping and rolling on the floor — to put him at ease. He coaches Elaine in a pouting, cute walk and fluting gestures, the very opposite of her athletic, free temperament. Bill makes faux marble for a desk and two columns; Mary Outten sews the costumes. Elaine's long ruffled muslin dress, fingers clenched in the photo; Fuller's tailcoat

A painter and a sculptor who have come for the summer complain about the students' lack of seriousness: they find themselves camp counselors. The painter, told to be tolerant of these young neurotics, draws himself up and declares: “I'm neurotic too”; he adds that he prefers New York, where hostilities go down into the subway and are filtered and diluted, to the direct hostility of BMC. The gesture: the painter plants himself, shoulders squared; he was then living in poverty
At the end of the summer: he had ten students, and six of them are leaving the college for New York. 6 students out of 10 leaving for New York

Before their year abroad, the Levis come back briefly to the community at the end of the summer session for the planned performance of M.C.'s translation of Erik Satie's The Ruse of Medusa, then leave for Europe. They leave without knowing whether they want to come back or whether they will be encouraged to. Consequences: Departure for Europe; M.C. speaks of the future as a dead end and of the idea of founding elsewhere a good place facing the future.

Rondthaler, Levi's ally, resigns as treasurer; Dreier announces that he no longer wants to be rector and is thinking of leaving. Dehn proposes Albers, elected without opposition after a discussion described in the minutes as spirited and inconclusive. Albers wants a small faculty, with newcomers appointed as “visiting teachers” without a vote for two years; the Levis protest in vain. Albers's condition: that Dreier stay. The official minutes: “spirited and inconclusive” Consequences: The Levis leave for Europe, the Rondthalers for Ocracoke; Albers becomes rector despite his distaste for administrative work

At the end of the summer, Albers to Bill: “You had ten students. Six of them are leaving... Do you know anything about it?” — “Sure,” Bill answers; he told them that to be artists they had to leave school, go to New York, take a studio, and paint. Albers does not seem to hold it against him. 10 students, 6 leaving for New York in September Consequences: Two years later, appointed head of Yale's art department, Albers hires de Kooning as his first artist
After deciding to resign, Dreier stays on at the college a little longer to ensure the transition to Josef Albers's leadership as rector. Consequences: Albers becomes rector of the college

At the end of the summer, Albers asks de Kooning (“Bill”) whether he knows that six of his ten students are leaving the college for New York in September; de Kooning replies that he told them that if they wanted to be artists, they had to leave school, come to New York, take a studio, and start painting. Albers does not seem to hold it against him. 10 students, 6 leaving; de Kooning's words as reported by Elaine de Kooning Consequences: Six students leave for New York in September 1948
Elaine leaves with a roll of enamel paintings on kraft paper — a tribute to the durability of paint; Bill finally finishes his single painting of the summer, “Asheville”.

The end of summer 1948: the two summer teachers complain about the students' lack of seriousness, feeling like camp counselors; the author suggests tolerance toward these young neurotics; the painter draws himself up, shoulders squared, and retorts. Words: “I'm neurotic too” — he has his rights too; and on New York: hostilities there go down into the subway, filtered, diluted, whereas here they are direct and immediate Atmosphere: End-of-session weariness, wounded pride Stakes: A conflict between artistic demands and the reality of immature youth

Knowing that single strips are insufficient, they all assemble the dome anyway; it stays slumped on the grass like wet spaghetti; the whole school has come to laugh in the rain Words: Bucky: “One never knows the ways of the Almighty” Atmosphere: rain, derision, a secret faith in the theory Stakes: the failure that heralds the dome's worldwide triumph
In the fall following the Black Mountain summer, Bill introduces Pat Passlof to Milton Resnick; they become a couple and marry in 1962. Consequences: The Passlof-Resnick marriage in 1962.

Enrollment falls from 90 to 50 students; no dietitian, no maintenance man, no business manager, no bookkeeper, no registrar; the Board of Fellows must immediately elect Schlesinger and Trayer to reach a quorum. A revised program is mailed to the students with an offer to refund deposits. 90 → 50 students Consequences: Most come back anyway; new staff quickly found

The complete list: Bodky (Style and Structure in Music), Guermonprez (weaving construction), Jalowetz (voice and bookbinding), Schlesinger (harmony and composition), Natasha Goldowski (chemistry and physics), Anna Goldowski (French and Russian), Frank Rice (German). Then Dehn comes back one weekend a month (mathematics and philosophy), Trayer gives “The Farmer and Society,” the Jennerjahns are promoted (printing; eurythmics). Sally by a student: the only non-European is Frank Rice — and he teaches German

A fire completely destroys the laboratory, along with the darkroom where Hazel Larsen had, contrary to her habit, stored many of her negatives. Everyone forms a bucket line, filling buckets in the dormitory bathtubs with antiquated hoses; Natasha goes in to retrieve explosive chemicals; the town fire department's telephone does not answer at first, and the building burns to the ground. The structure insured for less than $2,000 against a value of $12,000. Natasha carries on as best she can and adds a seminar on Our Destinies and Our Instincts. A building valued at $12,000, insurance < $2,000 Consequences: The loss of the laboratory, the negatives, the measuring instruments

Albers sets out his reorganization plan: concentrate the program on art and music, supplemented by selected academic subjects and practical work (woodworking, painting, bookbinding, construction for architecture students, agriculture), transfer administrative functions to professionals, and aim at 90 full-time students with about 15 teachers. Enrollment had fallen to about fifty students. 30 teachers needed for a full curriculum; 15 teachers planned; 90 students targeted; about 50 current students; instead of training only the intellect and memory, they regard the development of the will as their main task. Consequences: The basis of the contested reorganization plan.

Alex Reed, a weaving student in the mid-1940s, built with Molly Gregory the “Quiet House” in memory of Mark Dreier, the Dreiers' son killed in a car accident at the college; Reed remained close to the Alberses, almost a surrogate son.

Dahlberg leaves the college at the end of September 1948; Albers sums it up coldly in a letter to the Dehns (October 2, 1948): “Dahlberg has left. Could not endure it here.” Dahlberg demands explanations from Albers in several letters of August-September. Dahlberg-Zolli correspondence; Dahlberg to Homer Wall, September 3, 1948 Consequences: One departure in the 1948 wave

Olson's telegram to Albers on September 29, 1948, followed by an intense correspondence (Albers's letters of September 24, October 4, December 24, 1948, January 5 and 31, 1949; Olson's letters of September 30, October 7, November 6, 1948) to bring him to the college. Consequences: The decisive arrival of Olson, the future rector

The local fire station fails (a defective hose, according to Droll); an exchange of accusatory letters between Dreier and W. Dean Willis (December 28 and 30, 1948); the Board deals with the insurance on September 29, 1948; a new seminar meeting is held on October 5, 1948. a defective fire hose Consequences: Resentment against the local fire protection

After the fire in her laboratory in September 1948, the students design and build a science building for Natasha; she stubbornly refuses to set foot in it and holds her classes in her apartment at Meadows Inn; with her husband Eric, a former student, and her mother, she appears less and less in the dining hall and at public functions, becoming almost a recluse, before leaving for a small rented farm near Asheville Consequences: The trio isolated within the community

Ted Dreier announced his intention to leave by September 1948 at the latest, but was unable to tear himself away from a place in which he had invested so many personal, material, and spiritual resources.

The fire breaks out at the end of September; everyone passes buckets filled in the bathtubs with antiquated hoses; Natasha goes into the building and comes out with explosive chemicals; the fire department's telephone does not answer at first; the building is completely destroyed, along with Hazel Larsen's negatives. Atmosphere: Smoke, organized panic, Natasha's solitary courage Stakes: The material survival of the bled-white college

After letters in August demanding explanations, Dahlberg leaves; Albers announces it to the Dehns in one curt sentence; in February 1949, Dahlberg writes that Albers never answers his letters, then invites him to New York. Words: “Dahlberg has left. Could not endure it here.”; you never answer my letters… he is writing a book Atmosphere: hurt and literary irony Stakes: the impossibility of communication under the stress of the 1948 crisis

Albers appeals to the Whitney Foundation (letter to Rose of September 27, 1948) and works out a detailed reorganization in a 34-page projected program for 1949-1950 dated January 1, 1949 (with tuition and scholarship figures); he hopes to stabilize the college. 34 pages; another letter to Steinau of October 12, 1948, offering the post of “business director,” which Steinau declines Consequences: Rose replies on December 16, 1948; Forbes will decline

Josef reluctantly takes the post of rector of the college, which is going through faculty and funding difficulties. His first exhibition in Germany since the war, at the Galerie Herbert Herrmann in Stuttgart. Consequences: Growing tension with the institution

While waiting for an answer from the Whitney Foundation and other sources, Albers and Dreier go north to solicit friends. Forbes, who had often saved the college, leans slightly toward Levi's position, regretting the devaluation of letters. Consequences: A historic support falls away.

At the end of October, Albers proposes an outside governing body — a Board of Trustees, a mechanism BMC had scorned since its beginnings. Albers wants to stabilize the mentality of the place and have competent leadership, instead of everyone governing everyone except himself. It is the most contested element of his reorganization. Consequences: The fury of part of the community, Molly Gregory among them.

Having become rector in October 1948, Albers invites Isabel Mangold — who had left during the war — to come back as his secretary; she had written to him on January 8, 1948. Fred Mangold, professor of Romance languages and registrar from 1934 to 1942
The Watkins couple has a baby in October 1948, technically becoming a nuclear family without thereby fitting the dominant domestic model.
The previous fall, Tolk-Watkins and Rags Watkins drove across the country with Lanier to settle in San Francisco. Consequences: The Black Mountain network takes root in the Bay Area

In the fall, after North Carolina, de Kooning visits the Giacometti exhibition, with a catalog essay by Sartre. Elaine remembers: it overwhelmed him, it was crucial; it seemed the work of a civilization — not of a single man.
MoMA buys Painting, 1948
His defense of Matta and Brauner leads to his exclusion, noted in NÉON along with four other names. NÉON, 5 issues, 1948-9 Consequences: The first break with Surrealism

Two very brief notices on the back of NÉON no. 4 make public the exclusion of the painters and of the “Brauner faction”; Jouffroy will later evoke in his poems his own physical treatment by the Surrealists in 1948. notices on the back of the magazine NÉON, no. 4

The foundation announces that it cannot give funds in 1949: it prefers to support projects at their beginnings (as it had done for BMC) rather than on a continuing basis; it specifies that it does not disapprove of the college's development. Consequences: The college remains without major institutional aid.

De Kooning writes to the editor of ARTnews (published January 1949): on first entering Arshile's studio about fifteen years earlier, the atmosphere was so beautiful that he felt dizzy, and on coming to his senses he was lucid enough to take the hint at once. He is glad that it is almost impossible to escape Gorky's powerful influence, as long as he keeps it within him. The visit to Gorky's studio dates from around 1933-1934 (about fifteen years earlier).

The meeting of December 12-13, 1948; a New York meeting “on BMC” on January 14, 1949, according to Beaumont Newhall's notes; Dreier, in a telephone call to Trayer, is said suddenly to have judged that the college should close before the second term; Trayer reads a statement to the faculty on January 29, 1949; Duberman notes that Trayer, whose emotional stability was considered doubtful, may have amplified Dreier's pessimism after weeks of rumors of closing. Consequences: Fear of an imminent closing

Working on Attic, Bill hears Elaine say that the painting reminds her of Faulkner's forest; he lifts a pile of papers under which, as it happens, lay a book by Faulkner; Bill loved Faulkner's endless sentences, how many events fit into a single sentence Consequences: this belief in the expansive aspect of painting will mark Elaine's work

In the spring of 1949, Pavia organizes discussions and presentations by composers, philosophers, writers; after the lecture, fiery denunciations from the floor, then beautiful women pass baskets around to collect dollar bills, which buy liquor served in paper cups half an inch of liquor per paper cup; the polkas Pavia loved; dancing for hours

The following summer, Elaine wears her Frisette costume for this 21-minute silent comic film with intertitles: she plays the Witch (black wig, long frayed black dress), dances suggestively to Burckhardt's guitar, seduces him on the ground, then becomes Clarissa, the village coquette, waddling like a mechanical doll, dogwood blossoms in her hair. a 21-minute film; intertitles; the guitar played by Burckhardt

Elaine rents a studio in Provincetown and attends Hofmann's classes (Sunday-painting old ladies praised to the skies, young men sharply criticized) — a strange move, since she had found little of value in a past lecture; no doubt to get away from Bill and find a mentor. She retains his advice always to keep the ground and to add white when one gets stuck. She shares a house with Susie Mitchell (Greenberg's mistress) and the son of the owner of the Maeght gallery.
Hofmann, whom Elaine describes as a kind of bull elephant, gives a party with a punch, innocuous in appearance and of devastating alcoholic strength: everyone came out on all fours, she says.

According to Edith Burckhardt, when the others were hung over and gossiping, Elaine went cheerfully on painting and partying. At the end of the summer, her housemate asks her when it hits her: never, she replies — she would not allow it.

A humorous letter to her goddaughter (the daughter of Ernestine and Ibram Lassaw, named in her honor): swimming, boats, moonlight parties and picnics, the only person in Provincetown without a car; she sketches four painters' heads and a row of people holding ice-cream cones, and concludes that the days are getting shorter, adorned with musical notes (an allusion to September Song). sketches of ice-cream cones and musical notes

Every week, a painting “crit” draws a crowd of artists packed into the school's single room, heated by the sun through the skylight. Rivers lodges with his married mistress in a one-room apartment near the beach; he plays saxophone in a bar decorated with fishing nets; the summer is made of sex, nude bathing on the beach, liquor or pot, and painting. air full of fish and salt in town, an odorless breeze on the dunes

Guests: Elaine (arriving with Perle Fine), Schwartz, Klonsky, Fay Gold, Grillo, Tabachnick, Jane Freilicher — who brings her husband, a stack of Count Basie records, and tomatoes from her garden. Grillo cooks a dish that tastes like meat, admitting later that it was made of locally caught whiting. Elaine, heavily made up, in an unfashionably short skirt, talks fast about everything, from drawing to the death penalty, with her customary verve and intelligence. local whiting disguised as meat; Count Basie records
He came to see her now and then, Elaine admits. A photo shows them sitting back to back on the beach, Elaine in a sexy two-piece bathing suit, with a cheeky look. a two-piece bathing suit

Worried that Bill will drown after drinking sherry with an unidentified artist despite hurricane warnings, Elaine sees Sanders find them: the stranger is unconscious; to revive him, Bill and Sanders carry him toward the water and strip, having no bathing suits; a state policeman arrests them for indecency, a short spell in a cell until they sober up, a five-dollar fine. a $5 fine; sherry; a hurricane warning
Bill writes to Jack Tworkov to borrow fifty dollars so as to get back to New York and also leave a little money for Elaine — proof of his solicitude despite their separate lives. 50 dollars

Elaine dates the painting Bill was working on to a year after Black Mountain; Curtis proposes Attic. When Bill wanted to title a canvas “Interior,” Elaine had insisted on a specific room; Bill answered “Attic, because you put everything in it”. Possible confusion with Light in August (1946), after Faulkner.

A photo is captioned “early 1940s” in The Spirit of Abstract Expressionism, but in the film Strokes of Genius (1982) Elaine says it was taken in Provincetown in 1949. Bill's paintings inspired by that summer include Sailcloth and Two Women on a Wharf.
Albers begins the series in the summer of 1949, in Mexico; he will produce more than a thousand variations of the same image until his death in 1976. Three or four nested squares of different colors.

The architect William Bernard attends Josef Albers's classes at the National University of Mexico in 1949 and later acquires one of the paintings in the series; he sees in them schematic representations of rural Maya dwellings, with two doors in a rectangular facade. The dealer Francisco Rodríguez had acquired Albers's paintings in exchange for Mezcala stone figures; he would list them as “Casa maya”
With his first Homages to the Square, Josef chooses an even stricter diet, which will bear more splendid fruit.

After a few months of travel in Europe, Cruz and Piwonka structure a more defined program: an intuitive, abstract composition of three-dimensional space based on material, form, and color, a competence analogous to architecture, prior to it and necessary for it. the sequence of each quickly executed individual work: plans, model, critique, reconstruction of the model from the plans, group critique; the main difference from Albers: composition in predetermined spaces; published in Arquitectura y Construcción no. 16, p. 20, September 1949

Gropius commissions from Albers a mural as part of a three-million-dollar graduate center; Albers chooses Flemish bond, keeps the wall plain gray, and recesses voids into the brick to compose with shadows, up to 2.5 inches deep; he titles the wall América. Depth of the recessed bricks: about 2.5 inches; a passive horizontal order countered by an active vertical arrangement; void widths in brick lengths, half bricks, and fractions of 1/4 and 1/2 cut to measure. Consequences: A deliberate refutation of the Mexican muralists; a principle of economy through subtraction.

The architect William Bernard takes Albers's course at the National University in Mexico City in 1949 and later acquires a painting from the Adobe series; for him, these canvases evoke the plan of a rural Maya dwelling with two doors in a rectangular facade. a traditional Maya dwelling with two doors in a rectangular facade

Albers begins the Homage to the Square series, a reflection of his research on visual perception, the ambivalence of form, and the relativity of color. Consequences: This work will also influence Op Art and Minimal Art and culminate in the book Interaction of Color (1963) and the portfolio Formulation: Articulation (1972).

Gropius, as part of the program for the three-million-dollar Graduate Center, commissions a mural from Josef Albers; Albers creates a rhythmic pattern in the brick wall by withdrawing bricks to create recesses that play with the light. He chooses Flemish bond as the structural order, keeps the surface flat and gray, and has certain bricks recessed about 2 inches to compose with shadows. Cost of the building: 3 million dollars; bricks recessed about 2 inches; bricks sawn to exact measurements (lengths of 1/2 and 1/4 added to the existing modules) Consequences: Albers will reuse this procedure in Rochester (1967), in chimneys in Connecticut (1955, 1959), in the altar wall of St. Patrick's Cathedral in Oklahoma City (1961), and in a posthumous wall at Stanford (1980)

Resignation in February. A summer in Mexico (June 10 – August 15, Avenida Vera-Cruz 102 C, Colonia Roma) to forget education, administration, and community life a little (letter to Grote, March 31, 1949); four design seminars at the University of Mexico; three weeks with the Moellenhoffs; a possible visit to Anahuacalli with Rivera and Porset. The exhibition Anni Albers Textiles at MoMA (September 13 – October 30) — MoMA's first solo show of a textile artist; Philip Johnson commissions from her a drapery fabric for the Rockefeller Guest House. Josef paints his first Homage to the Square. Consequences: The end of sixteen years at BMC.
An exhibition of weavings at MoMA, the first museum on the list of selected solo exhibitions. Consequences: The consecration of textile art; press articles in October 1949

Albers leaves the college in 1949, believing that a colleague of one of the founders (himself) had been badly treated despite the promise to keep him on after a few years; several leave with him, and this is, in his view, the college's downfall. Consequences: Several people leave; the college's decline, according to Albers

Albers leaves the college in 1949; several people leave with him. He attributes his departure to members who thought themselves competent in everything and mistreated a colleague of a founder, despite the promise to keep him in his post after a few years. Several of them left, he says Consequences: Albers calls this departure the college's decline
The Alberses leave the college in 1949, after fifteen years there. 15 years Consequences: The end of an era

Another day, an errand to the Sears in Asheville: thirsty, she drinks at the fountain reserved for whites. Raised in Ohio, she knew Jim Crow but had never tasted the bitter flavor of white water. a “white” fountain, a Sears store

Cunningham comes in the spring before Litz: demanding physicality (raise your leg only if you can raise it all the way), the excitement of physical perfection, “dance by chance”. Litz arrives in the summer: what counts is what one feels when raising the leg, composition evolving from an organic source. These two polarized views form the basis of June's whole career. Consequences: Merce gave her the impetus of expression, Katie gave her the song

Schauffler bets two quarts of beer that Rondthaler will not go and settle in Oregon; Rondthaler takes the bet, moves, works for the Forest Service, graduates from Reed College, and makes a 35-year career there. two quarts of beer; 35 years in the Forest Service Consequences: settles permanently in Oregon; BMC friendships kept up
Jerry Wolpert, a BMC graduate, dies in 1949 in Buffalo, where he was teaching at the university. Consequences: Sue Riley remarries in 1958 and builds a career in early childhood education

Seven or eight students, including VanDerBeek (who arrived in 1949), interested in architecture and meeting weekly, work together for about a year, afternoon after afternoon, to design and build a “Minimum House”: to show that good design need not be expensive. A total cost of a little over a thousand dollars, the money provided by Paul Williams's mother, the stones for the walls gathered in the woods. Dr. Jalowetz's tombstone, with no particular shape or inscription, ends up built into the back wall. cost ~$1,000; stones from the woods; Jalowetz's gravestone in the back wall Consequences: an unintentional macabre incident

A long mimeographed report expressing the hope of a successful reorganization, while predicting a very different college, and stressing fifteen marvelous years and new paths that others will take up elsewhere A mimeographed document addressed to the “friends of the college”
A hostile student during the struggle of the first term, Mitchell discovers in the spring a transformed Albers, warm and kind, and with age develops affection, respect, and a sense of debt toward him

During the summer of 1949, Natasha becomes secretary and leads the search for new teachers, relying on Pittenger and on Aydelotte (her former boss at Swarthmore, Nell Rice's brother); Trayer serves as acting rector

Fuller accepts the direction of the summer session just after the resignations of Albers and Dreier; his usual fee has risen to $1,000 a month plus expenses, but he accepts what the college can pay The college pays him $800 for six weeks
Walley and Woelffer teach drawing, painting, and sculpture; their wives Diana Woelffer and Jane Walley run workshops in ceramics, jewelry, and photography

Fuller brings nine engineer-builders from the Institute of Design (one of them Black), who deride the local politicking; this time they put up a dome that holds and subject it to tests, with so little interest in the students' help that they are judged obsessed and Fuller inaccessible A fourteen-foot hemisphere of aircraft aluminum tubing covered with a Vinylite skin, worked on all year in Chicago; the dome flattens in September Consequences: Natasha stops speaking to Fuller at the end of the summer

Fuller throws a big party at which he co-opts a student with an impressive voice to read one of his two-hundred-page poems; although several guests doze off after the first hours, he cheerfully insists on finishing the reading A 200-page poem; a reading lasting several hours

Bodky directs the musical side of the summer session (while resigning from the faculty for the fall); the high point: a three-day Bach festival rivaling in intensity Cage's Satie marathon of the year before

Ehrman (weaving), the Jennerjahns (dance, printing), Nataraj Vashi and his wife Pia-Veena (Hindu dance, lectures on Hindu philosophy); Pait (philosophy and psychology) and Rosen, a physicist who had worked with Einstein, with Scholtz in symposia on infinity; visits from Langston Hughes and Bortai Bunting Bortai Bunting reveals that her family and Ezra Pound shared a house in Rapallo and that the youngest Pound might well be a Bunting
